Prime office rents rise in 3Q2026 as AI companies expand Singapore footprints
article:
Prime office rents in Singapore rose in 3Q2026 amid bolstered demand from AI companies and constrained supply of quality spaces, according to analysts.

CBD Grade A office rents rose 1% q-o-q in 3Q2026 to $12.32 psf per month, based on data from JLL. This brings cumulative growth for the first three quarters of the year to 2.8%.

Overall CBD office vacancy fell to 5.9% in 3Q2026. The figure is the lowest in 10 quarters, JLL added in a Sept 28 release.

Average CBD Grade A office rents and vacancy rates

This comes amid notable leasing momentum from AI and tech firms.  “What stands out this quarter is how decisively AI and technology firms are moving to secure space, even as broader macroeconomic headwinds remain unresolved,” said Michael Glancy, JLL’s country CEO for Singapore and Southeast Asia.

Earlier this month, US data-management firm Databricks announced plans to invest over US$350 million ($447 million) in its Singapore operations over three years and double its workforce to more than 500 employees.

As part of the expansion, the company will open a new 32,000 sq ft regional headquarters at IOI Central Boulevard Towers, quadrupling the company’s existing Singapore footprint. The new office is expected to open in November.

At the newly completed Shaw Tower along Beach Road, OpenAI is reportedly in advanced negotiations for approximately 120,000 sq ft of offices, according to JLL. The ChatGPT creator currently occupies roughly 100 desks at a co-working space operated by The Work Project at CapitaSpring in Raffles Place.

OpenAI rival Anthropic — best known for its Claude AI model — is set to open a Singapore office in October. The company is said to have taken up around 100 desks at The Executive Centre’s workspace at Ocean Financial Centre in Collyer Quay.

In a separate report, Knight Frank Singapore noted that other AI companies that have secured dedicated office spaces or expanded their presence include French company Mistral AI, US enterprise platform Sierra, and Meta-backed Manus.

“In the months and year ahead, more AI-related firms are expected to either move from co-working facilities to establish their own office space or set up shop directly in a CBD market where quality space options are becoming uncomfortably limited,” commented Tridiana Ong, head of occupier strategy and solutions at Knight Frank Singapore.

According to Knight Frank, rents of prime grade offices in the Raffles Place-Marina Bay area rose 1.5% q-o-q to an average of $11.87 psf per month in 3Q2026, while occupancy climbed 0.7 percentage points to 97.4% across the same period.

Average office rentals, by key precincts in 3Q2026

Shrinking large-format supply, growing flexible workspaces

Supply of quality offices, particularly large contiguous spaces, remains constrained amid limited new supply. In response, occupiers of such spaces are initiating lease renewals earlier, with some starting negotiations up to two years earlier to secure their space, noted JLL.

Some large occupiers are also exploring shifting from the CBD to the Orchard area, supported by the desire for a lifestyle-driven workplace to attract talent, Glancy observed.

One company making the move is Deloitte, which plans to relocate to Orchard Central in 2027, after its current lease at OUE Downtown on Shenton Way ends this year. In the interim, Deloitte will relocate a portion of its staff to a JustCo co-working facility at Orchard Point .

Meanwhile, Knight Frank highlighted that flexible workspace operators are also contributing to quality office demand. The firm estimates co-working spaces across Singapore currently total around 3.9 million sq ft, including JustCo’s newly opened Orchard Point centre, which spans 64,000 sq ft. The firm is also expected to open a new 16,000 sq ft centre at Raffles City Tower in January 2027.

‘Near-term scarcity’

With Newport Tower — the office component of City Development’s Newport Plaza in Tanjong Pagar — the only major completion slated for 2027, near-term scarcity of Grade A office space in Singapore will persist until new supply materialises in 2028, said JLL.

The firm has maintained its full-year forecast of 4% for CBD Grade A rental growth. It projects a cumulative five-year rental growth of 15% between 2025 and 2030.

Selected upcoming office supply islandwide

Knight Frank estimates full-year prime office rental growth will sit at the higher end of its 3% to 5% estimate for 2026.

The office market will remain supported by tight supply conditions in the last quarter of 2026 and going into 2027, said Knight Frank’s Ong.

As quality CBD offices continue to have rents “at a premium with no sign of easing”, companies would increasingly need to weigh the balance between prime spaces and more affordable options — such as older buildings or workspaces in fringe areas — over the next six to 12 months, she added.

title: Real estate private credit in Asia Pacific offers growing structural opportunity: CapitaLand Investment
article:
Real estate private credit in Asia Pacific (Apac) can offer asset-backed exposure and contractual income for institutional investors seeking resilience and stable income, in CapitaLand Investment’s (CLI) view.

“This growing opportunity is supported by tighter bank lending, low market penetration, borrowers’ evolving financing needs, and the increasing institutionalisation of real estate in Apac,” the Singapore-listed global real asset manager said as it released its latest research report .

Unlike corporate private credit, senior real estate private credit is secured against identifiable properties and underwritten against asset-level cash flows and values. Senior loans rank ahead of equity in the capital structure.

Contractual income, security over property assets, and priority over equity should therefore provide a defensive source of returns and portfolio diversification, according to CLI.

Another takeaway from its report is that the opportunity in Apac is structural, not cyclical.

While interest rates may affect borrowing costs, pricing and refinancing, and create near-term opportunities, the longer-term financing demand is being shaped by structural growth.

"Apac real estate credit also benefits from a gradual shift in the region’s bank-dominated financing market," CLI wrote.

"Without displacing banks, private capital can capture unmet acquisition and refinancing demand, supporting a sizeable and long-term investment opportunity as institutional allocations and borrower awareness deepen," it added.

Moreover, real estate private credit can provide a differentiated way to participate in the region’s major structural real estate themes: living and lodging, logistics, and data centres.

CLI noted that these three themes correspond, respectively, to trends in demographics and mobility, supply chain reconfiguration, as well as AI and digitalisation.

Across these sectors, repayment is generally supported by operating income in the case of stabilised assets and eventual refinancing or sale.

That said, the cash flows, collateral characteristics and execution risks vary materially.

Underwriting key Apac structural real estate themes:

There is no single playbook for the region’s real estate private credit landscape. Across developed Apac, markets differ in maturity and are evolving at different speeds, while property sectors have distinct repayment drivers and risks.

In particular, Japan’s property market is undergoing a structural shift. As of March 2026, there were about JPY147 trillion ($1.19 trillion) in outstanding loans to the real estate sector by Japanese financial institutions.

"To illustrate, even a 5% reallocation from traditional to private lending in Japan’s outstanding real estate loan market could imply an approximately US$46 billion ($58.8 billion) opportunity," CLI wrote.

Meanwhile, in Singapore, the city-state remains a highly banked market, though private credit complements banks to address specific needs, such as higher leverage, speed or structural flexibility.

Key developed Apac real estate credit markets:

Local presence and sector expertise are thus essential to origination, underwriting, monitoring and workouts, CLI said. Returns are expected to be driven by disciplined selection and structuring, not unfamiliar jurisdictions or unhedged currency exposure.

"Lending only in sectors where the manager has direct, through-cycle real estate experience results in more robust underwriting, structuring and managing potential stress," the research team added.

title: Vietnam and Panama to be removed from EU’s tax haven blacklist
article:
(Sept 28): The European Union is poised to remove Vietnam and Panama from its list of tax havens when EU finance ministers meet in Luxembourg next month.

Vietnam will be moved to a so-called “grey list” while Panama will be removed entirely, according to people familiar with the matter.

EU countries update the list of so-called non-cooperative jurisdictions twice a year. The function is meant to curb tax avoidance and encourage transparency. US territories Guam, Samoa and Virgin Islands, as well as Russia and Vanuatu, are among the other countries currently on the list.

Securing removal has been a top priority for Panama, its finance minister Felipe Chapman told Bloomberg in June. The country passed a bill in the summer meant to increase tax transparency and crack down on shell companies.

The Central American nation has been on the EU’s list of noncooperative jurisdictions — countries that score low on tax transparency and efforts to fight tax avoidance — since 2020, which has hurt foreign direct investment and business relations between Panama and the EU, Chapman said.

Vietnam, which is one of the fastest-growing economies in Southeast Asia, was added in February this year. The country will be moved to the so-called “grey list", which is used for countries that do not comply with international tax standards but have committed to implementing reforms. Jordan, Montenegro and Morocco, among others, are currently on that list.

See also: Indonesia pays first bond claim from pandemic-era guarantee

EU finance ministers are due to discuss the blacklist at a scheduled meeting on Oct 9 in Luxembourg.

title: Japan’s Takaichi touts sweeping changes in immigration rules
article:
(Sept 28): Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi took to social media over the weekend touting efforts to revise the country’s rules related to foreign nationals, days before some of those rules come into effect.

“The government acknowledges that some citizens feel anxious or a sense of unfairness due to the rising number of foreign residents,” she wrote in one of her posts, adding that the ongoing overhaul of rules is being implemented to “ensure order” and “enable both citizens and foreign nationals to live safely and securely”.

Takaichi listed a number of changes over a series of posts, also touching on some that have already been implemented, including stricter regulations for visas and a crackdown on illegal residents.

In what appeared to be an effort to show the fruits of the government’s efforts, she said there had been a 90% drop in visas issued in the “business manager” category in the first half of this year from a year earlier. She also said there had been a 15% increase in repatriations in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier.

Her posts come as new rules for permanent residents are set to come into effect on Thursday. Those guidelines include requirements for permanent residents to maintain an income level higher than the national average. Other rules in the pipeline include a requirement that applicants prove proficiency in Japanese and demonstrate an understanding of relevant rules.

“To ensure that both citizens and foreign nationals can live safely and securely, we will continue our efforts to achieve strict yet smooth immigration control and residency management,” Takaichi added.

See also: Growth minister says Japan has exited reflationary phase

The posts come as the government overhauls Japan’s policies concerning foreign nationals and immigration, ranging from plans to introduce a fee for travellers to Japan as early as 2028 to tighter visa criteria for those seeking to live and work in the country.

Surveys show that people are feeling uneasy about allowing more foreign nationals to reside in the country. A University of Tokyo survey released in August found that 56.3% of people polled in 2026 opposed having more foreigners in Japan, up from 35.6% in 2024. That survey found that the spike in sentiment against immigration was more pronounced among younger generations.

A separate poll by the Mainichi newspaper conducted in November last year found that 71% of respondents supported Takaichi’s efforts to tighten restrictions concerning foreign residents, compared with 10% who were against it.

title: China broadens travel curbs to encompass family of top AI talent
article:
(Sept 28): China has expanded overseas travel restrictions for top artificial intelligence (AI) professionals in private firms to include the families of key personnel, further tightening measures designed to prevent the outflow of critical know-how and information to the US.

Government agencies have recently begun to share the wider restrictions with affected people, which include prominent start-up founders as well as the heads of strategically important companies in AI-related fields, people familiar with the matter said. Direct relatives such as spouses and children of certain AI and chip executives, whose work is considered paramount to state security, are now required to obtain approval from Beijing before going abroad even for short trips, the people said.

That marks a broadening of existing curbs on the freedom of movement of China’s most influential tech talent — a category that encompasses entrepreneurs, researchers and executives. While not an outright ban on travel, the new requirement is likely to exert a further chilling effect on a tech sector already facing unprecedented curbs. China has restricted foreign travel for top AI professionals in private firms such as Alibaba Group Holding Ltd and DeepSeek since earlier this year, Bloomberg News reported in May, reflecting Beijing’s determination to safeguard its technology as it makes big strides in AI and chipmaking.

It’s unclear whether all those people’s families need to follow the new strictures, the people said. China is also separately implementing rules, which became effective Sept 15, for enforcing exit bans in cases ranging from criminal investigations to potential violations of the country’s industrial and technological security.

Beijing’s plan is to add relevant individuals to the list as time goes by, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing a sensitive issue. Government departments have already notified several people of the need to clear family travel, two of the people said.

Beijing has for years imposed travel restrictions on key personnel from prominent college researchers to nuclear scientists and executives at state firms, and their families are similarly affected.

See also: China’s consumer stocks face lost decade as AI steals spotlight

But the government is now specifically targeting talent within the private sector, as elite AI and technology engineers are considered strategic assets to the world’s second-largest economy. Much of China’s pool of top-flight AI talent emerged in the post-ChatGPT era — and mostly at the country’s tech giants or private start-ups.

The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology didn’t respond to a faxed request for comments.

Chinese officials’ fear of a potential outflow of key technology and talent intensified after Meta Platforms Inc’s US$2 billion ($2.56 billion) acquisition of Manus.

See also: Will these 21st-century Marco Polos return home with unbelievable tales?

The government eventually ordered the US firm to unwind the deal. As part of the fallout, Beijing moved to limit US investment in sensitive technology firms.

While the plan to restrict AI personnel’s movements isn’t necessarily linked to the Manus saga, guarding against technology leaks remains a key policy goal, Bloomberg News previously reported. Such a policy may force engineers with global ambitions to choose between staying home or going abroad earlier in their careers.

title: Bitcoin rally wobbles as macro risks overshadow ETF demand
article:
(Sept 28): Bitcoin continued to lose momentum on Monday, cooling after a blistering rally in recent weeks as a fresh bout of macro uncertainty weighed on risk assets.

The original cryptocurrency fell as much as 2.2% to US$82,702 before paring some losses. It remained below US$83,000 in morning trading in London.

Other digital assets also declined, with the second-largest token Ether down as much as 1.9% and Solana falling 3.7%.

The macro backdrop has weighed on cryptocurrencies. Crypto fell along with stocks and bonds after US President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s latest proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz while oil extended its gains. The moves come as markets are also digesting the Federal Reserve’s decision earlier this month to raise interest rates, with traders beginning to price a meaningful chance of another hike in October.

The pullback follows a rally early last week that briefly pushed bitcoin above US$87,000, its highest level since January. Institutional demand also picked up, with bitcoin exchange-traded funds attracting their largest weekly net inflows since the token reached a record above US$126,000 last October.

See also: Crypto exchange Bitget says hackers stole US$352 mil

Still, some investors see bitcoin’s recent weakness as a pause after earlier strong gains, rather than an end to the positive momentum.

“I don’t think the rally lacks conviction just based on weakness over the last few days, which would be expected at some point given the strength of late,” said Richard Galvin, executive chairman at crypto investment firm DACM.

US spot bitcoin ETFs attracted about US$2.4 billion in the week ended Sept 25, their biggest weekly haul since the period that ended on Oct. 10, when inflows topped US$2.7 billion. That came just ahead of a selloff that extended through much of 2026.

See also: Bitcoin bulls eye next leg as US$15 bil options expiry nears

The recent surge was enough to push the ETFs into positive territory for the year. After recording more than US$5 billion in net outflows through the end of July, the funds have since reversed that trend and are now approaching US$1 billion in net inflows for 2026.

Bitcoin has been on a tear over the past month. The token has surged about 28% since Aug 19, when the US Treasury said it would increase buybacks of long-dated bonds. Now it’s on track for its best quarterly performance since the fourth quarter of 2024, when the reelection of Donald Trump, who ran on a crypto-friendly agenda, helped Bitcoin surge 47%.

The move marks a substantial recovery from the first half of the year, although bitcoin remains well below its October high. The token has risen over 40% from July through September so far, reversing a 14% loss in the previous quarter.

Bitcoin had been relatively resilient in the face of recent developments seen as potentially detrimental to the industry. Beyond the Fed’s rate increase, the US Senate recently failed to advance the crypto-focused Clarity Act, legislation that was highly anticipated by crypto firms seeking clearer rules in the country.

Bitcoin is also becoming more intertwined with the broader treasury and liquidity environment. Higher Treasury yields — which are now higher than before the Aug 19 buyback announcement — can make non-yielding assets such as bitcoin less attractive, particularly when investors expect central banks to keep rates high.

“For bitcoin to break 2026 highs, it’s likely that the broader macro environment needs to be favourable," said Damien Loh, chief investment officer at Ericsenz Capital.

title: Erratic monsoon rain threatens India crop outlook, official says
article:
(Sept 28): India’s monsoon-sown crops are likely to have been affected by rainfall deficits in some areas and excessive precipitation in others, Farm Secretary Atish Chandra said.

The season was challenging at the start and water shortfalls would pose a challenge for winter sowing in areas that have experienced prolonged rainfall deficits, Chandra said at a meeting with state government officials to discuss preparations for the upcoming winter crop season.

The monsoon is crucial for India’s farmers because it irrigates fields and fills reservoirs that provide water for crops sown through the winter when there is typically less rain. India is a major producer of rice, wheat, sugar and cotton.

Water budgeting was a necessity, and winter cropping patterns would have to be planned based on availability, Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said at the meeting Monday.

So far this year, cumulative rainfall for the June to September monsoon season is 12% below the long-term average, according to the India Meteorological Department. If the deficit persists, it would be the weakest monsoon since 2015, when precipitation was almost 13% below normal. The weather office had forecast a 10% shortfall for this season back in May.

title: Indonesia pays first bond claim from pandemic-era guarantee
article:
(Sept 28): Indonesia’s government has paid bondholders the 722 billion rupiah owed to them after state-owned builder PT Waskita Karya failed to settle it last week, marking the first payout under a pandemic-era guarantee programme for securities issued by state companies.

“The total claim arising from the failure to repay the 722 billion rupiah principal” has been fully paid by the government and PT Penjaminan Infrastruktur Indonesia as guarantors, Tony Prianto, director of State Financial Risk Management at the Ministry of Finance, said in response to a Bloomberg query on Monday.

The government’s share was 610 billion rupiah and PII’s share was 112 billion rupiah, he said. Distribution of the funds to bondholders is scheduled for Monday, he added. The claim payment “does not constitute funding or additional financing provided to Waskita Karya” and it “does not extinguish Waskita Karya’s obligation,” said Prianto. PII is a state-run firm that provides government-backed guarantees for infrastructure projects and programmes.

Waskita is the first issuer to make the claim under a mechanism introduced in 2020 to support Indonesia’s economic recovery during the Covid-19 pandemic. The swift repayment shows the government’s guarantee programme is well funded to meet debt obligations of state-run firms covered by it.

Cleaning up these companies, including builders which accumulated large debts during former President Joko Widodo’s decade-long infrastructure drive, has become one of the challenges facing current leader Prabowo Subianto’s sovereign wealth fund Danantara as it seeks to restructure troubled state assets while preserving capital for new investments.

The government had set aside 6.45 trillion rupiah in reserves for guarantees under its National Economic Recovery programme, according to the 2026 budget documents from the Finance Ministry.

See also: HSBC makes big push for affluent clients in India to fuel growth

Waskita has allocated about 28.9 billion rupiah to cover interest payments on the notes and a separate bond issuance. Trustee PT Bank Mega had submitted the guarantee claim to the guarantors which had 20 business days after the scheduled payment date to settle it.

title: World’s top coal exporter strains to lift output as prices soar
article:
(Sept 28): Indonesia, the world’s biggest coal exporter, is failing to tap into soaring prices for the fuel as countries look to offset reduced natural gas supplies from the Persian Gulf.

At a conference in Bali, which is the highlight of the local industry’s calendar, traders are confronting some of the tightest supply conditions in years. Exports fell to a five-year low this month following the slashing of mining quotas by the government as well as low water levels at key barging rivers, DBX Commodities said in a note.

That comes as coal consumption is set to hit a record this year as demand is bolstered by higher gas prices — due to the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz — and a strong El Niño that’s increasing air-conditioning requirements, according to the International Energy Agency. Indonesian coal buyers, including China, South Korea and Japan, have already been observed switching from gas to coal in their power mix.

“Demand is shifting but the market remains tight from a supply perspective,” said Muhamad Fadhil, senior vice president at Argus Media, said on a panel at the Fastmarkets’ CoalTrans Asia conference. “Indonesia’s scale means lower production and exports could have an outsized impact.”

Benchmark Newcastle coal futures earlier this month rallied to their highest in almost two years, while in China — the top consumer of the fossil fuel — prices have reached levels not seen since 2023 after a deadly accident in May prompted a series of safety inspections that curbed domestic output.

See also: Copper slides as China industrial data weighs on demand outlook

With winter on the horizon in China, a shift to buying could have an immediate impact on the market. However, spot demand for Indonesian coal may be muted by high prices.

Jakarta has attempted to allow miners to cash in — using mid-year quota revisions to reverse earlier supply cuts that fell disproportionately on some firms. Some of those had to suspend production earlier this year and may take time to ramp up again.

Affected producers included PT Bayan Resources, one of the nation’s biggest miners, which saw its quota slashed earlier this year. It was raised days after a deal to sell a major stake to a tycoon close to Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto.

See also: US says China to buy 10 mil tons of coal in 2027, 2028

That transaction, along with the broader quota cuts and an attempt to force miners to sell at government-set benchmarks last year, undermined Indonesia’s credibility with foreign buyers.

“The uncertainty has created issues with us being able to purchase Indonesian coal,” said Matthew Boyle, head of research at trader Ashon International DMCC. “Last year we did about four million tonnes of Indonesian coal sales; this year we’ll be lucky to get two million.”

Meanwhile, there is ambiguity around the role of a new government oversight agency, Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia, which is meant to clamp down on practices such as under-invoicing that Prabowo said cost the state tens of billions of dollars. DSI President Luke Mahony on Monday tried to assure miners and traders that the body will merely monitor export prices rather than take full control of shipments.

“Let me be clear on one point: DSI is not here to disrupt the flow of Indonesian exports,” Mahony said. “Exporters will continue to export.”

title: Bond market is getting closer to sounding alarm on US economy
article:
(Sept 28): The bond market is on the brink of signalling that a series of US Federal Reserve (Fed) interest-rate hikes will start shifting the narrative towards the risk that the US economy stalls out.

The extra yield investors demand to hold 10-year Treasuries over two-year notes shrank to as little as 17 basis points last week, the slimmest gap since early 2025. This so-called flattening of the curve increases the possibility that the 10-year will soon yield less than shorter maturities, a closely watched phenomenon known as a curve inversion.

An inverted curve historically has offered a powerful signal: It has preceded each of the last eight recessions going back to the 1960s, although its predictive power proved faulty earlier this decade. It’s essentially bond investors’ way of showing they see the Fed pushing rates high enough to stymie the economy as it seeks to tame inflation. That outcome would have broad implications across financial markets, particularly for stocks trading near record highs.

It’s a scenario more investors are bracing for after the central bank raised rates this month for the first time in three years and indicated additional hikes are likely. It also drives home how the hawkish Fed is altering the balance of risks after a bond sell-off that reflected burgeoning price pressures against the backdrop of robust growth.

“Seeing the two- and 10-year curve invert or flatten dramatically calls into question the idea that the economy is very strong and that is part of what’s being priced into the bond market,” said Zach Griffiths, the head of investment-grade and macro strategy at the research firm CreditSights.

See also: US 30-year yield hits highest since 2004 as bond sell-off deepens

An inversion would reverse a global normalisation of yield curves seen since 2024. Bond investors tend to demand a higher return, or yield, for the greater uncertainty that comes with locking away their money for longer periods. That means yield curves usually slope upward.

As recently as last month, that was the trajectory for the curve as long-dated yields soared in part on worries that the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility was eroding under chairman Kevin Warsh. But after the central bank’s September hike, shorter maturities have led yields higher. Traders are betting on the equivalent of at least three quarter-point Fed hikes over the next year.

Some don’t expect the curve to invert soon as the amount of hikes already priced in makes it harder for shorter-term rates to rise further relative to longer-dated yields.

See also: Japan 10-year yield climbs to 1996 high as global rout deepens

“The market has already pencilled in significant Fed rate hikes, which have pushed the curve sharply flatter in recent weeks,” said Gennadiy Goldberg, the head of US interest-rates strategy at TD Securities. “This makes us believe the 2s10s curve is likely to move steeper in the weeks ahead.”

It’s also tough to envision the economy weakening significantly now. Economists just raised their forecasts for US third-quarter growth on stronger demand, according to the latest Bloomberg monthly survey.

But others say the flattening trend has legs. Ed Al-Hussainy, a portfolio manager at Columbia Threadneedle, said he’s positioning for an inversion of two- to 10-year and five- to 30-year curves over the next six months, as the Fed tightens policies to cool the economy and inflation.

“The best indication that monetary policy is getting tighter is a flattening and eventually an inversion of the yield curve,” he said.

In Asian trading on Monday, the two- and 10-year notes yielded roughly 4.90% and 5.21% respectively. The 10-year yield, a key global bond benchmark, is around the highest since 2007.

When the curve is inverted, it often reflects anxiety about growth prospects, given that rate hikes are designed to tackle inflation by cooling demand for loans. A growth slowdown could eventually set the stage for the Fed to lower rates, spurring long-term yields to fall relative to shorter ones.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Since 1978, the two- and 10-year curve turned upside down about 15 months before a recession started, on average, with the lag ranging from six months to two years, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.

The curve’s predictive ability, however, has faced increasing scrutiny in recent years. Various US curves inverted in 2022, with the majority of economists predicting a recession within 12 months. That never materialised as the economy proved largely able to withstand the Fed’s 2022-2023 tightening campaign, a regional banking crisis, a global trade war and this year’s surge in energy prices.

While the two- to 10-year curve is most frequently cited among bond investors, policymakers seeking a recession signal study others tied to three-month lending rates. The gap between three-month Treasury yields and 10-year rates remains relatively steep.

The recent flattening for two- to 10-year Treasuries has punished bond investors who came into this year positioned for a steeper curve. It’s also rippling through US stocks, especially bank shares. As banks typically borrow on a short-term basis and lend longer term, a narrower spread between the two erodes their net interest margins.

The KBW Bank Index, which tracks shares of the biggest lenders, fell into a technical correction last week, marking a 10% drop from its recent highs.

The move towards inversion reflects the potential for a complete shift in the economic outlook since the US war with Iran erupted in February. Before that, traders were betting on a series of rate cuts that would drag down short-term yields, instead of the hikes they are preparing for today.

An inversion “would be a sign that the Fed is making a policy mistake”, said Jamie Patton, a co-head of global rates at the TCW Group. “It’s raising rates too much, and it’s going to have to cut them hard in the future. So to us, inverted yield curves are not healthy signals for the macro economy.”

title: Copper slides as China industrial data weighs on demand outlook
article:
(Sept 28): Copper and other base metals retreated ahead of a weeklong holiday in China, as traders assessed the country’s demand outlook following slower growth in industrial profits.

Earnings at industrial enterprises rose just 4.2% in August from a year earlier, after increasing 11% in July, marking the weakest growth since the data showed a decline last November, according to the statistics bureau on Monday. China’s National Day holiday, meanwhile, runs from Oct 1 to 7.

Benchmark copper futures slipped as much as 1.6% on the London Metal Exchange, after capping a second weekly advance on Friday. The metal has rallied this year after bets the Trump administration will slap tariffs on refined metal triggered an increase in US imports, squeezing markets elsewhere.

While signs of supply tightness in the Chinese market have sustained copper not far from record levels, traders are closely monitoring macro drivers. Consumption and investment have softened, business confidence is sluggish and the government has kept the reins on fiscal spending.

In the US, investors largely expect a rate hike from the Federal Reserve in October, which would typically damp demand for industrial commodities.

Copper dropped 1.5% to US$14,397.50 a tonne on the LME as of 3.09pm in Singapore while zinc fell 1.5% and aluminium was 1.3% lower.

See also: US says China to buy 10 mil tons of coal in 2027, 2028

title: Singapore shares end higher as bank counters rise; STI up 0.3%
SGX Cares’ 2026 charity futsal raises S$150,000
